video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: How to Hold a Guitar Pick & Best Guitar Picks
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This beginner-focused tutorial surveys guitar picks and holding technique, recommending starting with ultra-thin nylon picks for ease of use and strumming. It introduces several pick options by thickness and material (including Dunlop USA Nylon 0.46 mm and 0.60 mm, orange Tortex, and the premium BlueChip) and explains how each affects control, click, and tone, especially on acoustic guitar. The video also demonstrates a holding method—having the pick exit from the side of the thumb for better strumming—and advises trying multiple picks at a store (buying about ten to compare feel). It notes that while picks simplify strumming and accuracy for beginners, some famous players don’t use picks, and players can switch to or away from picks as they progress.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Readiness Criteria to Move On to Lesson 2 — Memorize A and D Chords and Master Chord Changes
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this brief guidance, JustinGuitar outlines concrete criteria to decide when a beginner is ready to advance from Lesson 1 to Lesson 2. The core requirements are: memorize the A and D chords so you can form and identify them by feel without looking at a chart, and be able to change between those two chords at a steady pace (starting around 30 changes per minute, with a long-term goal of about 60 changes per minute). He emphasizes a practical timeline (most students can reach readiness in 2–4 weeks, with a hard cap of about 4 weeks). If progress stalls or boredom appears after a couple of weeks, it’s acceptable to move on to the next lesson to keep practice engaging, especially if you’ve also managed to play a song and maintain chord-change practice. He also notes that if in doubt, you can watch the final left-handed Lesson 1 video for reassurance before proceeding, and he signs off when readiness is confirmed.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: JustinGuitar Lessons & Songs App Global Launch — Feature Highlights
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This 53-second YouTube Shorts promo presents the global launch of the JustinGuitar Lessons and Songs app. The speaker highlights key features—backing tracks that sound like the original recording, a new interface, and alignment of the beginner course with the site—along with a free tuner and a giveaway of 10 free subscriptions. Viewers are directed to a link in the description to enter, and feedback is invited, with a closing note encouraging use of the tuner regardless of subscription status.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: How to Level Up Any Strumming Pattern | Guitar for Beginners
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this JustinGuitar lesson, the instructor reframes strumming as a flexible, musical skill rather than a rigid sequence. He emphasizes that players can add or omit strums without penalty, and that small, periodic variations (akin to drum fills) keep patterns sounding lively. The core guidance centers on building a relaxed, continuous arm motion as the foundation for all patterns, while encouraging the learner to experiment with different patterns, practice with a metronome to lock tempo, and incorporate dynamic control (soft to loud) and subtle pick-hand adjustments. The video also highlights practical habits: journaling preferred patterns, using a printable sheet from a previous lesson, and a disciplined 2-minute metronome practice per session to automate the strumming process and prepare for chord changes or singing.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Building a Personal Guitar Repertoire: Creating and Using a Songbook for Beginners
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s lesson advocates assembling a personalized repertoire songbook to support practice, performance, and collaboration. It walks through a practical workflow: use a display folder to hold printable lyric-and-chord sheets, compile your favorite songs into a single repertoire for regular practice, and share printed sheets with other musicians during jams. The video also covers portable digital options (saving PDFs in cloud storage like Dropbox for phone access) and emphasizes keeping a lean, manageable set of songs (around 20) to avoid overwhelm. The core message is that a well-constructed rhythm of physical and digital song sheets improves readability, memory, and the ability to play along with others, whether at home, at parties, or in gigs, with tools such as a dashboard or beginner app to organize songs.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: A Chord Tutorial: Open A Major with Alternative Fingering (JustinGuitar)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar's beginner lesson demonstrates an alternative fingering for the open A major chord. The tutorial shows placing the 2nd and 3rd fingers on the 2nd fret of the 4th and 2nd strings respectively, with the 1st finger tucked between them on the 2nd fret 3rd string, to produce a clean A chord with less pressure. It discusses muting issues, string-by-string checks (5th through thinner string), transitions to D and E chords, and common finger placement problems. The video also emphasizes quick, regular practice and introduces the 'Chord Perfect' approach for building chord confidence.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: A Minor Chord (Am) Tutorial: Fingering, Tuning Considerations, and Practice
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This JustinGuitar video teaches the A minor (Am) chord on guitar, starting from the A major fingering and showing how to transition to Am with a full finger change. It explains why Am can look like E major on a different set of strings, and why moving chord shapes down the neck is not a simple transposition due to guitar tuning—specifically, the B-string tuning pattern used in the 5th‑fret technique. The video pinpoints the key Am fingering (index on the 2nd string, middle and ring on the 4th and 3rd strings respectively) and notes that this same three-string layout is shared with A major. It also covers common alternative fingerings, cautions about muting issues (especially the open 5th string and the 2nd finger’s height), and closes with a practical practice method called “Chord Perfect Practice” that cycles through strumming and arpeggio picking to solidify correct fingering and future positions.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Relaxed, continuous strumming: practical guidance for developing feel
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar's video outlines a focused approach to improving strumming by emphasizing relaxation and continuous motion. The core idea is that keeping the hand moving makes many patterns feel natural, provided the player remains relaxed in the shoulders and mindset. The lesson blends practical drills with mood strategies: practicing with a metronome on a simple pattern (demonstrated on the C chord with a Down-Down-Up-Up-Down rhythm), resisting over-counting in favor of a smooth feel, and using a small repertoire of well-mastered patterns rather than chasing many patterns. A notable cue is smiling to reduce tension, framing playing as a feeling-driven act where the audience senses the relaxed performance. The guidance culminates in the beginner-friendly principle that relaxation and consistent motion are foundational to good strumming.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: The Most Common Strumming Pattern of All Time! Guitar for Beginners
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s beginner tutorial presents a foundational guitar rhythm: missing beat three within a down-strum pattern and the widely used alternate pattern “down, down-up, miss-up, down” aligned to a 1-2-and-3-and-4 count. He first guides a simple miss on beat three to train continuous right-hand motion, then demonstrates the full four-beat pattern (One, Two-and-Three-and-Four) at a slow tempo, emphasizing consistent pendulum-like wrist/arm movement and relaxed strumming. The lesson then stays practical: practicing with muted strings, using a metronome (80–100 BPM), and gradually applying the pattern to songs. He also covers equipment choices (prefer a very light pick for beginners), grip relaxation, and the mental approach to rhythm (counting aloud, staying relaxed to maintain groove) as a pathway from pattern drills to real playing.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Strumming the Right Strings for D and A Chords (Beginner Tips)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this beginner-focused micro-lesson, the instructor explains how to strum only the appropriate strings for common open chords, emphasizing that new players should aim to avoid the thickest strings on D and A chords while recognizing that early-stage mistakes are normal. For D, the recommended focus is on the thinnest four strings; accidentally striking the 5th string is discussed as acceptable, and hitting the thickest string is discouraged but not catastrophic during practice. For A, the thickest string is generally not played, though its E note is part of the chord, and the two exterior strings both produce E. The video stresses practical practice priorities—clean chord changes and a steady beat on the first count—over perfect string accuracy during early stages, and it frames the guidance as ideal considerations to bear in mind while pursuing Chord Perfect exercises and other beginners’ practice routines.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: JustinGuitar Lesson 5 Practice Routine: Finger Stretch, Chord Changes, Strumming with Metronome, and Song Practice
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This video outlines a structured 20‑minute practice routine for JustinGuitar’s Lesson 5, emphasizing foundational guitar technique and repetition to build accuracy and rhythm. The session starts with a two‑minute finger/stretch warm‑up, then a one‑minute C chord drill (Chord Perfect) followed by targeted chord‑change work (Am to C, then C to E minor). A two‑minute block focuses on strumming with a metronome and keeping timing consistent, then a two‑minute Come As You Are riff exercise. The video then moves into a 10‑minute song practice with suggested songs (Eleanor Rigby, Get Lucky, Black) aimed at reinforcing chord changes and rhythm. It also covers guidance on when to move on (memorizing the Note Circle and C chord, aiming for about 30 changes per minute, practicing at 80–100 BPM) and notes the upcoming G chord for the next lesson, with remarks on rhythm practice, potential play‑along resources, and the Beginner Song Course app as tools to reinforce timing and consistency.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Beat-1 Strum Readiness and Chord-Change Timing for Beginners (JustinGuitar)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this beginner-focused guitar lesson, JustinGuitar emphasizes the importance of getting chord shapes ready to hit the downbeat (beat 1) when strumming in 4/4 time. He demonstrates how to time chord changes so the new shape is ready for the next beat, uses an E→A example to illustrate one-strum-per-bar rhythm, and explains how players (including left-handed learners) can adjust the timing by starting changes around beat 3 if needed. The video also covers practicing with beat awareness: counting 1-2-3-4, tapping the foot, and optionally changing on beat 4 to improve rhythm. The takeaway is to prioritize a confident beat-1 strum and to use deliberate chord-change planning to sound musical while you learn.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: D Minor Open-Chord with Little-Finger Variant (Beginner Guitar)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This beginner-friendly tutorial teaches a D minor open-chord with an alternative fingering that uses the little finger on the third fret of the B string. The instructor contrasts this approach with the traditional 1-2-3 fingering, explaining why the little finger can be easier to position and how it helps the hand adapt to pressing strings. The video provides exact finger placements—index on the 1st fret of the high E string, middle on the 2nd fret of the G string, and the pinky on the 3rd fret of the B string—while emphasizing the standard practice of starting with an open D string (the 4th). It also covers common problems (muted 4th string, buzzing from the little finger), troubleshooting tips (using the 3rd finger if buzzing persists), and a relaxation-based drill to find a comfortable hand/arm position before strumming and checking the chord.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Air Changes: Simultaneous Finger Placement for Faster Guitar Chord Changes
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this JustinGuitar lesson, the instructor introduces Air Changes, a technique that speeds chord transitions by letting the next chord’s shapes form in the air and then land all at once on the fretboard. The transcript demonstrates how shapes can be pre-positioned before the change (with chords like C, D, G, E and A minor) and discusses when to lift or maintain an anchor finger. Viewers are guided through practical steps: start with familiar two-chord pairs, practice the air-changes, and then progress to time-bound drills (1-minute changes) to push speed while maintaining alignment of the fingers. The method emphasizes fluidity and consistent fingering over slow, stepwise finger moves, and notes that Air Changes can be incorporated early in a student’s progression as a consolidation tool, even though it’s not a strict Grade 1 requirement.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: E major open chord for beginners: fingering, strumming, and technique cues
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This JustinGuitar lesson teaches the E major open chord to beginners, focusing on exact finger placement (index on the G string 1st fret, middle on the A string 2nd fret, ring on the D string 2nd fret), and why the second finger sits slightly back from the fret to accommodate the third finger. It demonstrates strumming all six strings and introduces a strum–pickup–strum practice pattern, with options to use a thumb for picking notes. The video also covers thumb placement behind the neck to build muscle for barre chords, common beginner issues (muting, pressing too hard, and proper finger-tip contact), string-by-string troubleshooting, and the importance of memorizing the chord shape before advancing in the course.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Guitar TAB Basics: Six-String Layout, Frets, Chords, and Rhythm Essentials
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s beginner-focused tutorial introduces guitar tablature (TAB) as a practical alternative to traditional notation for guitarists. The video explains that TAB uses six horizontal lines representing the six strings, with the bottom line corresponding to the thickest (low E) string and the top line to the thinnest (high E). Numbers on the lines indicate frets to press, while a zero means the string is played open. The presenter demonstrates a C-like idea of fretting across the six strings by showing an E major-like layout (0-2-2-1-0-0) and explains that notes can be played on multiple strings, so rhythm in TAB is not shown by default. He also notes that fingering isn’t specified by TAB—the learner must apply logic or follow guidance—emphasizing that early TAB literacy is a valuable skill. The video concludes by contrasting TAB’s lack of rhythm notation with the importance of listening to a riff or song for rhythm and by recommending that beginners begin reading TAB as soon as possible.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: JustinGuitar Beginner Course Grade 1 Introduction — Lesson Structure, Fundamentals, and Practice Routine
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This 1:15-long opening video from JustinGuitar introduces the Beginner Guitar Course Grade 1 by explaining that lessons are structured like private sessions, and that the first lesson covers essential fundamentals beyond technique (reading chord boxes, holding the guitar, and how to hold picks). It also outlines a full daily practice routine and notes a left-handed learning option in the Nitsuj series. Because remote learning precludes in-person tuning, Justin instructs that students must learn to tune their guitar themselves, with tuning addressed in the next lesson.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: All About Guitar Capo: Types, Placement, and Key-Change Techniques
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This JustinGuitar lesson explains what a capo is, how it changes pitch and allows open-position chord shapes to be used higher on the neck, and compares popular capo designs. The presenter demonstrates two brands (Kyser and a compact G7th), discusses how to position a capo just behind a fret for clean tuning, and shows practical uses: playing songs in easier keys with familiar chords, transposing songs to fit a singer’s range, and using capo to match original recordings or play along. He emphasizes that capo use is valuable for beginners and for more advanced players alike, and he cautions about tension affecting tuning. The video includes a walk-through example using Walk of Life to illustrate transposition and singing with capo, plus rough voice-range guidance and tips for trial-and-error placement.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Note Circle, Sharps, Flats, and Enharmonic Equivalents — Beginner Guitar Theory
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s lesson introduces the note circle (the chromatic twelve-note system), the concept of octaves as duplicates across the fretboard, and the basic wiring of natural notes (A–G) with sharps and flats. The video defines enharmonic equivalents (notes that sound the same but have different names, such as A# and Bb), explains semitone and tone (whole-step) as steps around the note circle, and uses practical guitar references (e.g., the 12th fret octave cue and the 5th-fret A example) to map semitone movement to frets. It also covers why some intervals do not have sharps/flats between certain pairs of notes (B–C and E–F) and how spellings like B#, Cb, E#, and F can be equivalent to other notes. The content is framed as foundational music theory for beginners and as a precursor to more advanced theory later in the course.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: How to Pass JustinGuitar Grade 1: Core Targets and Practice Guidelines
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this instructional video, JustinGuitar outlines the practical targets a beginner must meet to pass Grade 1 of the JustinGuitar Beginners Course. The core requirements include tuning with a tuner, memorizing eight basic chords (A, D, E, A minor, D minor, E minor, C, G) and playing them from memory with good tone most of the time; achieving rapid chord changes (30 changes per minute, i.e., about 2 seconds per change); using a steady 80 BPM strumming pattern with a metronome; memorizing five easy songs with simple progressions and performing them for real or via recording; and optional Ear Training Grade 1 and Music Theory Grade 1. The video emphasizes self-assessment, achievable pacing over weeks, and progress-oriented celebration rather than formal external testing. It also encourages recording oneself to reveal and address weaknesses and stresses a forgiving, enjoyable learning mindset.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: 6/8 Strumming Pattern with Missing Beats (1, 2 and 3, 4, 5 and 6) – JustinGuitar
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this JustinGuitar lesson, the instructor introduces a concrete 6/8 strumming pattern by first establishing the feel of 6/8 with a down-strum on every beat and an accent on beats 1 and 4. He then demonstrates a distinctive variation that omits beats 2 and 5, resulting in the counting 1, 2 and 3, 4, 5 and 6 (and the alternates shown for 1, 2 and 3, 4, 5 and 6). The hand continues moving even when a beat is skipped, and the pattern is rendered as Down, Up, Down, Down, Up, Down, with an optional extra upstroke after beat 6 to extend the groove. The video emphasizes slow, deliberate practice, maintaining continuous motion, and gradually increasing tempo, with encouragement to apply the pattern to 6/8 songs and to experiment freely within the rhythm framework.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Interval Ear Training for Beginners: Getting Started with Ear Training in JustinGuitar
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s ear-training video introduces beginners to Interval Ear Training as a standalone, beginner-friendly module. It explains why ear training matters for musicianship, outlines how interval awareness strengthens listening and helps singing, and describes a practical path into the module (starting with recognizing simple intervals, using familiar melodies to anchor the sound, and attempting basic tests to track progress). The presenter emphasizes that ear training is optional, but beneficial for overall musicianship, and notes that even some professional players excel without formal ear training or music theory. The video also frames interval work as a training gym for the ear and previews how later steps in the course build toward singing in tune and identifying melodies or chords on the guitar.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Guitar Holding Technique for Beginners: Stabilize with the Forearm, Not the Neck
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: The video presents practical guidance for beginners on how to hold the guitar so the fretting hand doesn’t bear the neck. It emphasizes keeping the guitar stable with the forearm and body pressure, explains how instrument balance can vary (neck-heavy vs body-heavy) and why that matters for control, and contrasts acoustic and electric grip approaches. The presenter also notes the importance of a relaxed, non-tensed posture, and even suggests ergonomically minor cues like rolling up sleeves to improve grip sensation. Overall, the lesson aims to establish a solid, comfortable playing position that minimizes wobble and supports clean fretting during practice.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Angle, Grip, and Forearm Mechanics for Beginner Strumming (Acoustic vs Electric)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This lesson presents beginner strumming mechanics with a focus on relaxed forearm motion, arm placement on the guitar, and pick handling for both acoustic and electric guitars. It emphasizes keeping the arm resting on the guitar to reduce shoulder tension, driving strumming from the forearm rather than the wrist, maintaining a near-parallel hand to the strings, and using a loosely held, thin pick. The instructor then contrasts acoustic and electric setups, noting differences in rest support and comfort, and closes with guidance on adapting mechanics to individual anatomy and instrument size. Practical tips include adjusting pick angle (a slight downward tilt from the thumb), minimizing tension to avoid a harsh sound, and progressive use of thicker picks as control and volume improve.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Open-String Note Names on Guitar with Mnemonics (E A D G B E)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This JustinGuitar lesson teaches the note names of the guitar’s open strings and introduces mnemonic devices to help beginners memorize them. The core mnemonic presented is Eddie Ate Dynamite Good Bye Eddie, mapping to the open-string notes E–A–D–G–B–E, with explicit verbal confirmation of the sequence. The video also discusses alternative mnemonics (including a humorous older variant and a community-driven example) and notes that mnemonics can be self-created to suit the learner. Beyond the primary mnemonic, the instructor emphasizes the importance of remembering open-string names as a foundation for learning the fretboard, clarifies string numbering (string 1 is the thinnest, string 6 the thickest), and mentions potential ambiguity caused by two E strings when using certain naming conventions. The lesson culminates with guidance to memorize the open-string notes before advancing to the next lesson, and cross-references a related Music Theory course for further mnemonic experimentation.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Learn ANY Strumming Patterns with this Guitar Exercise
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this JustinGuitar lesson, the instructor explains a practical framework for rhythm guitar in 4/4 time that unlocks the ability to create and recognize strumming patterns. He demonstrates how there are eight potential strums in a bar (down on each beat and up on each “and”), emphasizes keeping the hand moving even when not actively strumming, and introduces a circle-beat method for mapping patterns. The video covers pattern variation, including a common pattern nicknamed “old faithful” (down down up up down) and how to manipulate patterns by shifting which beats are strummed. He provides player-focused practice tips, such as starting with beat one, practicing slowly, then increasing tempo, and eventually playing without chords to automate patterns. The lesson stresses feel and groove as the ultimate goal, and connects pattern work to real songs and playing with others, with additional resources available on the website.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Easy Minor Chord Songs with Am, Dm, and Em — Practice Guide from JustinGuitar
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s short guide centers on using the D minor chord (and related Am and Em variants) to practice a curated set of songs across genres. He highlights specific examples where Dm and Am carry the progression (notably Arctic Monkeys’ “505”), notes minor/blue-influenced passages (Ain’t No Sunshine, All Your Love), and calls out songs with other chords such as E major and E minor (Chocolate Jesus, A Girl Like You). The video emphasizes practical tips for chord changes, tempo control (slow practice for speed of changes in Fallin), and the importance of motivation by choosing songs you enjoy. It also points to supplementary resources on the website (song lists, Beginner Song Course app, play-along tracks) to support ongoing practice.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Stopping Between Chord Changes? Here's How To Fix It!
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this JustinGuitar lesson, the core message is to avoid stopping the rhythm when changing chords, a habit that makes mistakes obvious to listeners. The instructor explains that “forcing the changes” to happen on the beat—while keeping the strumming continuous—preserves the groove and makes errors less noticeable. He demonstrates how rhythm can vanish when you stop, and advocates practicing with a metronome, drum grooves, or backing tracks to build solid timing. A structured practice approach is offered, including a one-minute-changes drill to push speed, the use of play-along songs (via the beginner song course app) for real-world feel, and tools like the JustinGuitar Time Trainer. The takeaway is that rhythm drives music, beat-one alignment is essential, and consistent tempo will improve chord-change speed over time.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Two-Chord Practice: A and D Chords for Beginners (Dance The Night Away & More)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar's beginner-focused tutorial demonstrates practicing with songs that use only two chords, A and D, to improve chord changes and rhythm. He explains that the early days will be challenging, advises selecting songs with minimal chord changes or slowing the tempo, and promotes using his Beginner Song Course app to tailor speed and accompaniment. The video spotlights the two-chord pattern in Dance The Night Away by The Mavericks (D for a bar, then A for a bar, repeated) and mentions additional two-chord options such as Born In The USA, You Sound Good To Me, and Silence Is Easy. It also covers anchor finger technique, counting and strumming on the beat, and the value of play-alongs—both in-app and on the website—for a more song-like practice experience. The message emphasizes persistence, a practical 10-minute practice window, and forgiving oneself during the early learning process.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: C Major Chord Essentials: Fretting, Muting, and Relaxed Technique (JustinGuitar)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This video educates beginning guitarists on forming the C major chord with an emphasis on accurate finger placement, muting the low string, and maintaining a relaxed fretting posture. The instructor walks through the proper fretting order (index on the 2nd string 1st fret, middle on the 4th string 2nd fret, ring on the 5th string 3rd fret), then addresses common challenges such as muting the thickest string, avoiding string buzz, and ensuring the 4th string rings clearly. Additional guidance covers finger-angle, the tip-focused contact of the fretting fingers, minimal hand gap, and the importance of a relaxed arm and shoulder to accommodate individual hand shapes. The video also outlines a practical approach to practicing chord changes (e.g., maintaining a hand-off and re-landing the fingers) and foreshadows future transitions to chords like G and D.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: 6/8 Time Signatures for Beginners: Counting, Feel, and Strumming (JustinGuitar)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s tutorial introduces time signatures with a practical focus on 6/8. It explains that time signatures describe the feeling of beats in a bar, contrasts the common 4/4 feel with 6/8, and clarifies that 6/8 comprises six beats per bar arranged as two groups of three, with beat 1 as the strongest and beat 4 as a secondary emphasis. The video guides beginners to hear and count 6/8 by listening to sample songs, counting 1–6 (and their ‘ands’), and to practice with a metronome at a moderate tempo while emphasizing the downbeats on 1 and 4. It also covers practical strumming strategy in 6/8, including six down strums per bar, the use of subdivisions, and an upcoming lesson on a specific 6/8 pattern. A variety of song examples are suggested to reinforce the feel, and the instructor cautions about different approaches for left-handed practice while encouraging attentive listening and internalization of the rhythm.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: JustinGuitar Lesson 2: Practice Routine (Chords, Anchor Finger, and Song Practice)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In JustinGuitar’s Lesson 2: Practice Routine, Justin walks through a structured 20-minute beginner-friendly practice sequence designed to build chord accuracy, finger independence, and timing. The plan emphasizes four practice sessions per week, cautions about finger pain and overdoing it, and then steps through a chord-focused drill (E, A, and D chords) before a dedicated anchor-finger exercise that cycles through chord shapes. The routine includes short, timed drills on each chord, a pattern-based transition exercise, and a riff-focused segment (Peter Gunn theme) to develop picking and finger agility. A 10-minute song practice follows, prioritizing songs the student enjoys (notably Three Little Birds) and, for now, avoiding capo; tempo and rhythm targets are discussed, including keeping a steady rhythm with foot tapping and aiming for roughly 30 chord changes per minute in early stages. The module ends with guidance on when to progress, the importance of memorizing chords before moving on, and pointers to practice-along resources and the website for further materials and updates.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Two-Finger G Chord for Beginners (HACKED!): A JustinGuitar Demonstration
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this beginner-focused guitar lesson, JustinGuitar demonstrates a simplified G chord that uses only two fingers, designed to be easier for novices than the traditional three-finger shape. The core setup places the 2nd finger on the 3rd fret of the low E (thick) string, which also conveniently mutes the 5th string, while the 4th, 3rd strings remain open and the 3rd finger frets the 3rd fret of the high E string. A comparison to the standard traditional G—where the 1st finger lands on the 2nd fret of the 5th string—is offered, with an emphasis that the traditional voicing can sound muddy and complicate chord changes in common progressions. The video emphasizes muting technique, finger placement, and tone, and presents a practical practice exercise called “Chord Perfect” to ensure the 5th string stays muted. The host suggests learning the two-finger version first and returning to the traditional shape later if needed, noting smoother transitions especially when moving from C or D chords. This analysis captures the instructional steps, tone considerations, and practical practice guidance described in the transcript.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: JustinGuitar Practice Assistant: Build and Track Guitar Practice Routines (Free)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This video is a practical walkthrough of the Practice Assistant feature in JustinGuitar’s platform. It demonstrates setting up a new routine, creating and editing practice items (for example 'Chord Changes' with a metric like 'Number of Changes'), and how to attach related links and statistics. The presenter shows item-level actions (edit, duplicate, archive) and adds items from the site (such as finger gym) into routines, then refreshes the page to reflect changes. The tutorial covers managing multiple routines, making one active, starting a practice session with a countdown, and using notes, a metronome with tempo and subdivisions, and end-of-minute alerts. It also explains how to record statistics (e.g., chord changes), switch between items mid-practice, import preset routines ( Blues Licks ), and view overall practice stats with graphs. A closing note highlights that the Practice Assistant is free and invites support via a donation button.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Intro to Up Strums: Pattern 1 and Pattern 2 for Beginners
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this beginner-friendly lesson, JustinGuitar introduces the first strumming pattern that includes an up strum after beat 2, showing how to count and execute it with a muted guitar neck and a pendulum-like forearm motion. He emphasizes slow, repetitive practice to develop a smooth, automated rhythm, explains how the up strum interacts with the beat (including the non-full-string nature of the up stroke), and offers practical guidance on staying in time even if chord changes falter. A second pattern adds a second up strum within the bar, followed by a discussion of tempo, relaxed technique, and the importance of repetition. The video foreshadows the most common pattern, nicknamed “Old Faithful,” and suggests applying these patterns to simple chords like A minor and E minor, with a reminder to practice rhythm (not just chord changes) and to use the Beginner Song Course app for pacing in time.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: How to Strum a Guitar WITHOUT a Pick
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s beginner-to-intermediate guide explores strumming on guitar without a pick, focusing on finger-style options, tonal variation, and practical patterns. The lesson covers why players might avoid a pick, contrasts fleshy-thumb tones with nail tones, and methodically demonstrates several approaches using the thumb or the first finger (alone or combined), including how to angle the hand to avoid strings catching, how much arm versus finger motion to use, and how to blend thumb and finger techniques for different song needs. It presents common patterns such as bass-notes on beats 1 and 3 with a down/up strum on 2 and 4, backbeat feel, and the concept of mixing strumming with fingerstyle to add melody and rhythm. The video emphasizes comfort, musical context, and the idea that there isn’t a single “right” method, encouraging self-observation, experimentation, and tailoring technique to the song and player level (with a nod toward more advanced, percussive fingerstyle later in the journey).

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Module 5: C major chord, strumming foundations, and basic theory
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar's Module 5 Beginner Guitar Course lesson introduces the C major chord (noting its stretchiness), then moves into strumming fundamentals, including how the 'overall picture' of strumming works and how to add extra strums to craft patterns. The video then shifts to a light theory segment: the note circle, sharps and flats, and the 12-note scale, followed by practical practice strategies such as compiling a personal songbook. It ends with a hands-on riff workout using Nirvana's Come As You Are to illustrate applying chords and strumming to a real song context.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Are You Strumming on the Beat? — 4/4 Timing, Down Strums, and Counting (JustinGuitar)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar's Are You Strumming on the Beat? explains how to play in time with a 4/4 bar by focusing on a downward strum on the beat, counting 1-4, and coordinating a foot-tap with hand strumming. The lesson emphasizes practicing with muted strings to establish a solid downbeat, developing an automatic coordination between hand and foot, and building a strong internal tempo rather than relying on complex upstrokes. It also covers practical pacing for songs, offering simple variations for faster tempos (strumming only on beat 1 or two strums per bar on beats 1 and 3) and stressing repetition, gradual progression, and realistic expectations for beginners.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Up Strums for Beginners: Thin-pick technique, muted practice, and thinnest-string focus (JustinGuitar)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This JustinGuitar beginner lesson explains up strums (upstrokes) as the in-between motion to the standard down strum. The video emphasizes using an ultra-thin pick to facilitate clean upstrokes, teaching muted practice to avoid noise, and clarifying that upstrokes typically strike only the thinnest three or four strings. Through slow, counted practice (one-and-two-and-three-and-four-and) with optional foot tapping for rhythm, the instructor guides learners to coordinate rhythm with the strum direction, gradually transitioning from muting to actual strumming on the guitar. The lesson also contrasts strumming all strings versus focusing on the thinnest strings for clearer, more musical results, especially when working with common chords like D minor and A minor. A preview of upcoming strumming patterns that incorporate upstrokes signals progression beyond the basics.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Beginner Open-Chord Songs: Eleanor Rigby, Get Lucky, and Pearl Jam
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this JustinGuitar video, the instructor curates beginner-friendly songs that align with the course’s open-chord focus, emphasizing C and Em while noting that G will be introduced in the next lesson. He highlights Eleanor Rigby as a first choice using C and Em, with a nod to interesting chord changes during barre sections and the flexibility to vary strumming patterns. He also covers Get Lucky by Daft Punk as a simplified, repetitive strummed progression based on Am–C–Em–D, pointing out D as a common hurdle. A brief mention of Pearl Jam illustrates how some favorites fit the course via chords already taught, specifically using C but not G. Viewers are encouraged to pick one song or rotate among several, and to check a website-listed set of recommended songs. Overall, the video emphasizes chord familiarity, careful changes, and practical strumming across recognizable tunes.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Struggling With Rhythm? Try my NEW Guitar App! :)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this JustinGuitar video, the instructor introduces his Lessons and Songs app as a companion to the beginner course, highlighting features designed to accelerate progress: a free built-in tuner, a large library of playalong tracks (over 600 songs), and a structured learning path with song recommendations aligned to Grade 1 and Grade 2 material. The core instructional emphasis is rhythm training through continuous backing tracks to prevent bad habits like stopping between chords, thereby improving both chord changes and timing. The video also shows practical app usage—how to navigate the learning path, use the practice assistant to plan practice duration, filter songs, and operate playback controls (swipe to slow, scrub forward/backward). It previews upcoming features (website-app syncing, simpler MIDI-based backing tracks, and more guidance) and reinforces the app’s credibility with positive reviews from App Store/Google Play. A practical takeaway is that the app is presented as a real-time practice partner that complements the course to reinforce rhythm, consistency, and progress tracking.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: How to Read Guitar Chord Diagrams: D Major Basics
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar's beginner-friendly tutorial introduces how to read guitar chord charts. It explains the anatomy of a chord diagram—six strings, frets, and the nut—with discussion of how the nut may be drawn, how lines indicate frets, and how the neck is depicted with finger-placement dots. The video also covers how to read finger numbers (1=index, 2=middle, 3=ring, 4=pinky) and the notation T for the thumb, as well as X for muted strings and O for open strings. Using a D major diagram as the first example, it demonstrates the exact fingering: first finger on the second fret of the third string, second finger on the second fret of the thinnest string, and third finger on the third fret of the second string, with the remaining strings muted or open as indicated. This lesson establishes foundational skills for reading chord shapes in subsequent lessons.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: E minor chord (Em) from E major — left-hand lift and third-string emphasis
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This short JustinGuitar lesson demonstrates forming the E minor chord by lifting the index finger off the G string (the open G string marks the minor quality when the other fingers hold the E major shape). It emphasizes a common muting issue: if the third finger (ring finger) settles too flat, it can mute the G string and obscure whether the chord sounds major or minor. The instructor stresses keeping the index finger’s contact with the G string on the tip, so the G string can ring clearly, and notes that the critical cue for the Em sound is the ringing of the third string during any strum. The video then guides a quick practice check: when strumming, ensure the third string rings out rather than relying on a full six-string strum, reinforcing a practical approach to distinguishing E major vs. E minor by ear and finger placement during basic chord work.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: 8 Essential Open Guitar Chords: Revision and Technique
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this revision-focused lesson, JustinGuitar revisits eight essential open chords (D, A, E and their minor forms Am, Em, Dm, plus C and G), emphasizing solid fretting technique, tone, and muting accuracy. The talk highlights fingertip placement, keeping fretting close to the frets, and avoiding muting unwanted strings—especially the thicker and thinnest strings across chords. Practical tips include starting downstrokes from specific strings to avoid unwanted notes, and keeping the thumb behind the fretboard during early practice. The video also discusses common beginner pitfalls (such as the third finger muting the thinner string on D, or muting the thinnest string on A) and notes the learning curve of D minor. A recurring theme is the strategic practice approach—focusing on the chords that feel hardest and using the linked chord lessons to reinforce accuracy—culminating in the “Chord Perfect Practice” routine to raise overall consistency across all eight chords.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: One Minute Changes: Speed up A–D chord changes
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: The video introduces the One Minute Changes exercise, a speed-focused drill that alternates between two chords (A and D) for one minute to build faster, smoother chord changes. It emphasizes anchoring a finger, tolerating some inaccuracy early on, and using a timer while counting each change aloud to quantify progress. The instructor differentiates One Minute Changes from Chord Perfect Practice (speed vs. tonal accuracy) and suggests practical targets: around 30 changes per minute as a pass threshold and 60 changes per minute as a long-term goal, with the expectation that some chord changes will be harder than others. The video also promotes supplementary tools (a practice routine generator and a One Minute Changes counter app) and references left-handed practice (Nitsuj lessons) as a relatable starting point for beginners. Viewers are encouraged to log progress and discuss results in the comments.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Music Theory for Guitarists: Practical, Fun and Fast (JustinGuitar)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar argues that music theory is a practical, beginner-accessible tool for guitarists that serves as a shortcut to faster, better music-making. He contrasts theory’s practical utility with traditional classroom approaches, emphasizes chord manipulation from a single grip, and explains how understanding chords within a key accelerates learning and improvisation. He links ear training with theory for stronger results, introduces Sus chords as a theoretical substitute, and covers basics like notes, sharps/flats, and the major scale. The video also notes that Grades 1–2 are free as an entry point to his paid Music Theory Course and encourages songwriting once playing is possible, while acknowledging that theory isn’t mandatory for everyone.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Anchor Finger Chord Changes (E, A, D): E to A and E to D using the anchor finger technique
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This video demonstrates an anchor-finger approach to smooth chord changes among E, A, and D on the guitar. The technique centers on keeping the first finger as an anchor while sliding it between frets to form the target chords, then dropping the remaining fingers into place (2 and 3 for A or D). The presenter walks through E→A and E→D transitions, emphasizes sliding the anchor finger first, returning to E, and adds guidance on practicing in finger order (1-2-3) and a suggested one-minute drill to build familiarity with the motion before speeding up changes. The guidance focuses on feeling and pattern rather than introducing new guitar shapes beyond those three chords.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Peter Gunn Theme: Beginner Riff, Finger Exercise & Picking Technique
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar presents the Peter Gunn theme as a beginner-friendly riff that doubles as a finger and picking exercise. The lesson demonstrates a specific four-finger fretting pattern (1st finger on the 2nd fret, 2nd on the 3rd, 3rd on the 4th, and the little finger on the 5th) played on the thicker string with the open-string notes forming the pattern Open, Open, 2, Open, 3, Open, 5, 4. He emphasizes hand position, finger spread, and consistent pick-hand motion (downstrokes) while practicing even eighth-note rhythms (counting 1 and 2 and 3 and 4). The video also covers muting to prevent unwanted string ringing, discusses common beginner pitfalls, and frames the riff as both a musical exercise and a confidence-building practice routine. A left-handed version is referenced (Nitsuj Series), and Justin notes the pace is faster than most beginners can comfortably play, encouraging steady practice and perseverance. The overall aim is to develop finger independence, timing, and picking accuracy beyond simply memorizing the riff.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: G Chord for Beginners: Song picks, 6/8 rhythm, and dynamics
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This JustinGuitar lesson centers on selecting beginner-friendly songs that feature the G major chord (the new chord introduced in Lesson 6). It showcases concrete song options (including Unknown Legend and Hey Joe) to practice G along with related major chords, and it explores 6/8 timing with This Year’s Love while highlighting other G-inclusive tunes like Mad World and County Roads. The host emphasizes practicing with simple chord progressions (C, G, D, A, E), using left-handed practice, and maintaining motivation by choosing songs learners truly enjoy, with a note that the next lesson will consolidate skills and sustain momentum.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: How to Hold a Guitar: Posture, Leg Position, and Arm Support (JustinGuitar)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This instructional video guides a beginner through practical guitar holding and posture to minimize strain and facilitate chord changes. Justin explains a right-handed player should typically place the guitar on the right leg (with an optional left-leg classical setup), how the forearm should rest and support the guitar rather than the shoulder bearing the weight, and the importance of relaxing the arm to avoid fatigue. He notes differences for acoustic (forearm sits on top) versus electric (forearm rests on the front), and suggests sleeves or fabric can affect grip. A stable, cutaway–torso interaction helps the instrument stay in place, while not leaning across the neck and maintaining an upright posture reduces risk of wrist, neck, and back discomfort. The narrative also covers practical cautions such as avoiding leaning to look at fingers, and the possibility of using a strap as an alternative support.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Strumming Dynamics for Beginners: Transform Your Play with Sectional Dynamics
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s Strumming Dynamics for Beginners teaches how deliberate dynamic shaping—varying volume, texture, and phrasing across song sections—can dramatically improve guitar performance. The lesson anchors dynamics in a familiar song structure (verse, chorus, bridge) and emphasizes that there is no single universal strumming pattern; instead, players should differentiate sections (quiet verses, loud choruses) and cue the listener toward repetition and sing-along moments. Practical guidance includes lifting into the chorus, using bridges for contrast, and repeating the chorus to maximize hook impact. The video also covers live vs. recorded contexts, the role of drums and cymbals in signaling dynamics, and an exercise to record oneself, compare extreme dynamics versus a flatter performance, and learn by studying favorite music. Learners are encouraged to apply these concepts to any song form and to listen critically to their own performances and to music they love for dynamic artistry.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: G Chord Cheat, Alternate Picking & 6/8 Time (JustinGuitar Module 6)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this 79-second JustinGuitar beginner lesson (Module 6), Justin introduces a simplified G chord fingering described as a “cheat” to make the shape easier and sound better, then moves into an overview of alternate picking and basic picking mechanics. The lesson also includes foundational music theory by explaining time signatures with a focus on 6/8 time and its rhythmic feel (often associated with a waltz-like feel), followed by a practical note on naming the notes on open strings and a technique for forcing chord changes to keep playing along. He concludes with a preview of the week’s songs, tying together technique, rhythm, and practical playing for beginners.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: JustinGuitar Grade 1 Practice Routine – Consolidation and Song‑Focused Plan
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This video outlines a practical, editable practice routine aimed at consolidating Grade 1 skills. It emphasizes targeted chord-change drills for the weakest pairs, two minutes of 4/4 strumming with a metronome, deliberate work in 6/8 time, riffs for fun, and a strong emphasis on playing songs. The host also recommends a potential finger-stretching exercise, tuning practice as needed, a self‑test after a period of study, and a philosophy that prioritizes solid foundations and enjoyment of the learning journey over rushing to the next grade.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Your First Strumming Pattern: Beat-1 Strum in 4/4 Time (JustinGuitar)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s beginner-focused lesson introduces the foundational strumming pattern by teaching players to strike on the first beat of a 4/4 bar. The video explains that early material uses 4/4 time (four beats per bar), shows how to count 1–2–3–4, and then guides the learner to strum down on beat 1 while keeping the hand moving on beats 2–4. It emphasizes coordinating chord changes with beat 1, acknowledges common early-week difficulties, and suggests practicing with a backing track or the Beginner Song Course app to reinforce the on-beat strum. The aim is a solid, repeatable beat-1 strum as a foundation for playing songs, with a realistic progression from beat-1-only strumming toward fuller rhythm once coordination improves."

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Strings Ringing Out Between Chord Changes
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this instructional piece by JustinGuitar, the host explains that open strings ringing between chord changes is a normal, often audible phenomenon in guitar playing. He notes that such strings frequently appear on the up-strum after beat four, especially at faster tempos, and may go unnoticed in real-time. The guidance emphasizes keeping the strum light on the thinner strings, slowing down to hear the effect, and maintaining a relaxed, tension-free approach to changes to preserve musical ease. The lesson also encourages listening with the ears, accepting that some “wrong” sounds can be aesthetically pleasing in creativity, and reassures learners not to be upset by occasional open-string noises during changes.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Master 3-Chord Songs with A, D, E: Capo, Play-Alongs, and Beginner Song List
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This beginner-focused guitar lesson centers on using just three chords—A major, D major, and E major—to play a wide range of songs. The instructor discusses practical strategies for practicing with a limited palette, including using a capo to align with original recordings, and relies on play-alongs from a dedicated app or website. He catalogs example songs that fit the A-D-E framework (and some that use only A and D), highlights Three Little Birds as a particularly suitable 3-chord tune, and emphasizes choosing material you love to maintain motivation. The video also directs learners to a Spotify playlist and a website page with song lists and additional resources, and it promotes integrating drum/bass/m melody tracks to focus on chord changes and strumming practice.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Understanding Open Minor Chords: E Minor and A Minor, and the One-Note Change from Major
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this beginner-friendly JustinGuitar lesson, the host explains what minor chords are in relation to major chords, demonstrates open E major and E minor, and shows how minor forms typically differ by a single note (such as G# changing to G). He then walks through A major to A minor, notes the occasional D major/minor consideration, and emphasizes that chord voicings on the guitar often reuse the same three notes with doubling when strummed over six strings. The video underscores the audible difference between major and minor chords, offers ear-training tips for recognizing them, and covers notation conventions (maj vs m) while planning to cover D minor in a later lesson. Practically, the lesson reinforces keeping the first finger movement minimal and prioritizing familiar open shapes (E minor and A minor) to build early fluency in minor chords.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Alternate Picking for Beginners: Angle, In/Out Motion, and Downward Pickslanting (JustinGuitar)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This JustinGuitar lesson introduces beginner-friendly alternate picking on single strings, focusing on how the pick’s angle and a deliberate in‑toward/outward motion affect efficiency and speed. The host demonstrates how a flat pick tends to catch and how a slight angle (around 20 degrees) lets the pick glide over the string, then emphasizes a practical in‑toward/outward motion (about 45 degrees) to ease string crossings. The video also presents the concept of Downward Pickslanting, credits Troy Grady and his Cracking The Code site, and suggests experimentation with different grips and anchor points (e.g., little finger) while keeping the practice goal simple: just alternate picking on one string to develop feel and control. Aimed at beginners, the lesson blends technique tips with a clear, patient practice plan and points to further resources for faster picking.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: JustinGuitar Lesson 3 Practice Routine – 20-Minute Structured Practice Focus (A minor / E minor)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This lesson guides a beginner through a compact 20-minute practice routine centered on the A minor and E minor chords. It starts with chord-perfect practice for clean voicings, then progresses through a sequence of one-minute chord-change drills (A minor to E, E minor to D, and A minor to E minor), followed by a focused anchor-finger drill. A 2-minute strumming segment emphasizes a relaxed arm and steady pick technique, then a 2-minute riff practice on Seven Nation Army targets muting and string awareness. The session concludes with 10 minutes of song practice using the two-chord progression, offering song choices (Sing, Moves Like Jagger, I Belong To You) and guidance on pacing, chord-change speed targets, and the optional use of the Beginner Song Course app to build timing and confidence.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: How to Play the D Chord on Guitar
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar's beginner-oriented tutorial teaches the D major chord on guitar by guiding the learner through the exact three-finger shape and placement order: index finger on the 2nd fret of the G string, middle finger on the 2nd fret of the high E string, and ring finger on the 3rd fret of the B string. The video emphasizes placing fingers close to the frets, angling the knuckles, and avoiding muting by keeping the fingertips on the tips of the strings. It covers common beginner challenges such as finger pressure timing, muting issues on the open 4th string, and maintaining the thumb behind the neck to support future barre chords. A four-stage practice framework, called Chord Perfect Practice, is introduced to help learners lock in correct finger placement, refine tone through small adjustments, and solidify the strumming pattern.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Beginner Finger Stretch Exercise for Guitar: Four-Finger Fretting and Down-Picking
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This video presents a beginner-friendly finger-stretching drill for guitar, delivered by JustinGuitar. The instructor emphasizes slow, controlled stretching rather than speed, framing the exercise as a cross-string fretting pattern that develops finger independence, reach, and precision. The core drill starts with the first finger on the 5th fret of the thickest string and adds the 2nd, 3rd, and little finger in sequence, then moves the pattern across to the 5th string and repeats. Alongside the left-hand work, the video introduces an all-down-picks right-hand approach and discusses anchoring the little finger while picking, with guidance on keeping fingers close to the frets and maintaining a palm alignment parallel to the fretboard. The instructor notes common anatomical variations (e.g., 2nd/3rd fingers tending to stay together; 1st/little finger splaying) and stresses a forgiving, patient approach for beginners. A practical practice prescription is given: about two minutes per day for one to two weeks, gradually increasing difficulty by shifting closer to the nut as comfort grows. The lesson also covers left-handed demonstrations, addressing common early struggles, and ends with encouragement and a reminder that progress comes with consistent, mindful practice across weeks.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Memorizing Easy Guitar Songs: Focus on Repetitive Chord Progressions (4-5 Song Repertoire)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this 2020 JustinGuitar video, the host presents a practical method for memorizing simple songs on guitar suitable for social settings. He emphasizes choosing tunes you enjoy that use very small numbers of chords and learning the chord order so you can perform from memory without a songbook or searching online. The approach centers on repetitive chord progressions, avoiding songs with varied verse/chorus patterns, and building a short repertoire—about four to five easy songs—that you can recall reliably at parties. The guidance also recommends delaying the inclusion of more complex pieces until you’ve established a solid recall baseline and feel comfortable with the simpler material.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Foot Tapping for Guitar Beginners: How to Keep Time by Tapping Your Foot
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: In this JustinGuitar lesson, the instructor explains why players tap their foot to establish an external pulse that helps them keep time while playing guitar. He emphasizes that the heartbeat is not a reliable tempo source, and introduces the idea of using a metronome later in the course. The video covers where and how to tap—preferring a heel tap with the left foot for right-handed players to avoid the guitar jumping and disrupting chord changes—and discusses alternatives (toe taps, standing or seated tapping, even unconventional body movements). A core message is to practice tapping along with music to develop a subconscious sense of beat, with practical homework such as tapping any time there’s music (excluding car scenarios) and gradually integrating rhythm with chord changes and picking. The lesson culminates in guidance on public pacing and the long-term beginner journey from finger pain to rhythmic accuracy.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Anchor Fingers for Fast A-D Chord Changes
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s lesson centers on the anchor finger technique to speed up chord changes, specifically between D and A chords. The instructor emphasizes keeping fingers light and in position, using the first finger as an anchor while the other fingers lift and reposition, and sliding the anchored finger forward to place the remaining fingers for the A chord. The practice is performed without full pressing or strumming to develop a fluid, rapid transition, with guidance to relax the fingers and avoid tension. The video foreshadows longer-term progression with the concept of 'One Minute Changes' after mastering the anchor approach.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Welcome to Module 3: Capo, Minor Chords & Up Strums
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This beginner-oriented module focuses on rhythm as a core guitar skill while expanding chord vocabulary with minor and E minor. The instructor frames the lesson around two new chords (minor and E minor), reinforces the importance of solid strumming and timing, and touches on the typical beginner pain timeline as practice continues. The transcript indicates an emphasis on rhythm over perfect chord accuracy and sets the stage for applying capoed transpositions and new chord shapes in subsequent lessons.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Using a Metronome for Consistent Guitar Timing: 80 BPM Start and Down-Strum Practice
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This JustinGuitar tutorial demystifies the metronome and demonstrates its value for beginner guitarists. It defines what a metronome is, explains BPM (beats per minute), and contrasts wind-up analog devices with digital options and mobile apps. The video highlights using an app-based metronome (specifically the Justin Guitar Time Trainer Metronome) and sets 80 BPM as a practical starting tempo. Viewers are guided to align a simple down-strum with the beat, optionally tapping a foot to the tempo, and to avoid rushing or anticipating the click. The instructor emphasizes that timing is a core musical skill that improves with steady metronome practice, including its application to various strumming patterns. A portion of the lesson invites learners to experiment with metronome practice beyond the first weeks and to use the Justin Guitar app as a convenient practice tool.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Practice Common Chord Changes: Song-Based Prioritization and 1-Minute Drills
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: JustinGuitar’s short tutorial centers on practicing common guitar chord changes efficiently. Rather than drilling all 25 changes in isolation, the approach advocates selecting 5–6 songs you want to play, analyzing the chord changes within those songs, identifying the most difficult transitions, and prioritizing practice around those. The plan emphasizes a practical, song-driven method (including a social test at a party or barbecue) and notes that some changes (such as D to Dm) may be postponed until they appear in a chosen song. A 1-minute-per-change drill is mentioned as a benchmark, used to justify focused, efficient practice rather than rote repetition of every possible change.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Module 4: D minor, finger stretches, and strumming refinements

The segment concludes by signaling that the finger-stretching exercise will be revisited in the next lesson.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Strumming: How to Practice Counting the Beats | Guitar for Beginners (rhythm counting with 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and)
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This JustinGuitar lesson focuses on building rhythmic accuracy for strumming by counting in 4/4 time and integrating the “and” between the beats. The video frames rhythm work as foundational to the course, with the instructor highlighting the importance of staying “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and” rather than sloppy, disrupted timing. A future section hints at adding the up-strum as the next step in the technique progression.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: JustinGuitar Lesson 1 Practice Routine — 20-Minute Daily Plan
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This video outlines JustinGuitar’s Lesson 1 practice routine for beginners, prescribing a 20-minute daily practice window with a recommended four sessions per week (daily if possible). video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Lesson 7: Air Changes, Consolidation & Grade 1 Review

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Three Tips to Avoid Guitar Finger Pain (Beginner)

The transcript maps these suggestions to concrete verbal instructions and timing cues throughout the video.

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Minimizing Finger Pain via Correct Guitar Finger Placement
video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.summary: This JustinGuitar lesson demonstrates how finger placement within a fret affects the amount of pressure needed to produce a clean note, with a practical exercise to train beginners to minimize finger pain. The session guides the learner through a controlled exercise: place the first finger on the fifth fret of the third string, pluck with the thumb to assess note quality under light pressure, then move the finger toward the back of the fret to feel the increased effort required. video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: JustinGuitar Lesson 4 Practice Routine: Finger Warm-ups, D Minor Focus, Strumming, Riff, and Song Work

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: How to Tune Your Guitar for Beginners: Clip-on Tuners (PolyTune and Snark) and Basic Techniques

video-justinguitar-grade-1-beginner-guit.title: Em to Am Focus: 3 Easy Songs for Beginners (JustinGuitar)
